tts: Have I ever told you about the camping experience we had in France? This happened about ten years ago, when the kids were really young. We had been camping in the south of France in our camper van, and we were on our way home. We had booked into a campsite outside Paris, just for one night, to break up the journey.

We reached the suburbs of Paris at about three in the morning. The kids were fast asleep in the back. I was driving and Liz was reading the map — this was before satnav. But she was doing a rubbish job of navigating and we kept getting lost.
I was getting more and more annoyed with her, and in the end she threw the map at me and said “OK, you find the campsite” — and then fell asleep.
I carried on driving, but I was exhausted. So when I saw a big empty car park by the side of the road, I thought: forget the campsite, I will just park here for the night.

Next morning I woke up and I could hear children’s voices. Lots of them. So I got up, opened the door, and you will never guess what I saw. Hundreds of children, staring at me. You know what I had done? I had parked in a school playground.

items.q: Why did the family stop in a car park?
o: They were lost and the driver was exhausted

items.q: What had actually happened?
o: He had parked in a school playground
He had parked on a motorway
He had parked in a private garden

items.q: When did he find out?
o: The next morning, when he heard children’s voices

acts.title: Learning Holidays
tts: It is eight in the morning and I have just arrived in St Ives, one of Britain’s most famous seaside towns. I caught the Riviera Sleeper from London late last night, and woke up a world away from the hustle and bustle of the capital.

This small fishing town in the south-west corner of England is home to some of the most stunning scenery in the country. While the climate cannot compete with Spain or Greece, its spectacular coastline and long sandy beaches have made it one of the most popular beach resorts in Europe.

But not all holidays are about taking it easy. I have not come here to spend my weekend sunbathing; I have come here to paint. I have not picked up a paintbrush since I left school, but I have come here to develop a new skill I can take home with me.
Artists have always been attracted to St Ives. In the 1930s and 40s the town was a centre of creativity, attracting many talented artists. Today it is home to one of the world-famous Tate museums.

The St Ives School of Painting was originally opened in 1938 by two trained artists who had met as soldiers during the First World War. In 1948 the school purchased the Porthmeor Studios, which had been used by St Ives artists for over sixty years.

This weekend we are concentrating on still life, and because it is a mixed media weekend we are looking at various styles and techniques, including drawing, printmaking and oil painting. There are never more than eight students, so teachers have a lot of time to explain and demonstrate.

items.q: Why has the presenter come to St Ives?
What is St Ives known for besides its beaches?
o: Its art scene, including a Tate museum

items.q: When was the School of Painting opened, and by whom?
o: In 1938, by two artists who had met as soldiers

items.q: What does she say about class size?
o: There are never more than eight students

tts: St Ives is in the south-west corner of England, and its long sandy beaches have made it one of the most popular beach resorts in Europe.
The presenter had not picked up a paintbrush since she left school.
The school was originally opened in 1938. In 1948 it purchased the Porthmeor Studios, which had been used by St Ives artists for over sixty years, and which sit on the edge of Porthmeor Beach.
There are never more than eight students in a class, and building confidence is central to the school’s philosophy.
The course begins at nine forty-five on Saturday morning and ends on Sunday at three. She bought a paintbrush as a memento rather than sweets or souvenirs.

acts.title: Reacting to a story, and complaining about one
rule: English speakers expect a listener to make noise. A story told into silence is a story the teller assumes has failed, so the reactions are not decoration — they are what keeps the other person talking. Written complaint works on the opposite principle: no reactions at all, and one clear request.
points: Match the reaction to the emotion. A funny story wants That is hilarious; an infuriating one wants I bet you were furious.
You’ll never guess what happened. And then, to make matters worse… To cut a long story short…
State what happened, in order and without adjectives. Then say what you want.
Yours sincerely when you know the name; Yours faithfully when you wrote Dear Sir or Madam.
eg: You’re kidding!
Surprise. Works for good news and bad.
That is hilarious!
Only for a funny story.
I bet you were furious!
Only for an infuriating one.
You must have been so embarrassed!
A past deduction, used as sympathy.
I’m not surprised.
Agreement — and slightly flat, so use it carefully.
You’ll never guess what happened.
Opens the biggest moment of your story.
To cut a long story short, they had cancelled the flight.
Jumps to the end.
And then, to make matters worse, they lost my luggage.
Adds one more problem.
I am writing to complain about the service I received on 14 March.
The standard opening line of a complaint.
I would therefore request a full refund of the ticket price.
The standard closing request. Say the number.
acts.careful: A complaint that only describes the problem is not a complaint; it is a story. The last paragraph has to say exactly what you want to happen next.

use: I am writing to complain about…

write.q: Write an email of complaint of about 180 words about a journey that went wrong — a flight, a train, a hotel, a delivery. Give the events in order using the past simple and the past perfect, name one thing that made it worse, and finish with one specific request. Use the correct closing for the greeting you choose.
plan: what you are complaining about, and when
write.model:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to complain about flight KC908 from Astana to Frankfurt on 14 March, and about how the delay was handled.

The flight was scheduled for 09:20. By the time passengers were told anything, we had been waiting at the gate for three hours, and the information screens had still not been updated. Staff at the desk told us twice that boarding would begin in twenty minutes.

To make matters worse, when the flight was finally cancelled at 14:40 we were directed to a rebooking desk that had already closed for the day. I reached Frankfurt twenty-six hours late and missed the meeting the trip existed for.

I am aware that a technical fault is nobody’s fault. The three hours of silence were, and so was the closed desk.

I would therefore request the compensation payable under EU Regulation 261, together with the cost of the unused hotel booking, which was 148 euros.

I look forward to your reply.

Yours faithfully,
Tilek Nurlanov
